prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN) -- A massive anti-Mafia sweep that stretched from New York to Sicily has not only cut off the head of the Gambino crime family but lopped off "the shoulders and chest" too, prosecutors said Thursday. John "Jackie the Nose" D'Amico, shown in 1992, is one of 62 people indicted. Sixty-two members of the Gambino, Genovese and Bonanno families face 80 charges, ranging from money laundering to illegal gambling and murder. "These charges strike at the very core of the Gambino family," said Benton Campbell, United States attorney for the Eastern District of New York. The Gambino family profited from extortion within the New York construction industry and its labor unions, according to the charges.  Watch the perp walk » . Several companies allegedly paid a "mob tax" in return for "protection" and "permission to operate," said Gordon Heddell, inspector general of the U.S. Department of Labor. Other charges involve an alleged illegal gambling ring, said Richard Brown, Queens County district attorney. Nicholas Corozzo -- a reputed captain in the Gambino family -- was involved in a sports gambling enterprise that relied in part on toll-free telephones, Brown alleged. Meanwhile, four members of the Gambino family are charged with eight crimes involving murder, according to the indictment. Those charges include the felony murder of Jose Delgado Rivera, who was shot and killed in an armored truck during a robbery in 1990. "Today we are able to bring closure to crimes from the past that have never been forgotten," Campbell said. He said the crimes span back over three decades.  Watch feds say they've 'cut off the head' of crime family » . Key to the Gambino arrests Thursday was a member of the Attorney General's Organized Crime Task Force who infiltrated the Gambino family and recorded hundred of hours of conversations, said John Milgrim, a spokesman for the attorney general. Forty-five of those charged are already in custody, police said. Arrests were made in New York City; Long Island, New York; and New Jersey. "It is as unrelenting as weeds that continue to sprout in the cracks of society," New York Attorney General Andrew Cuomo said of organized crime. "We will not rest until organized crime is a distant memory." In addition to the arrests in the New York area, police in Italy detained 77 people in connection with organized crime. Those arrests netted important members of a powerful clan in Sicily linked to Mafia boss Salvatore Lo Piccolo, who was believed to be the successor of the boss of bosses, Bernardo Provenzano.  Watch the prosecutor explain why authorities acted now » . Police say that in his attempt to rise to power, Le Piccolo tried to mend fences with New York-based Mafia families after those ties were broken during the bloody Mafia wars of the 1980s. Those families included the Gambinos of New York and the Inzerillos of Italy. Provenzano was arrested two years ago in Corleone. "It is evident that the intent of the Mafia in Palermo was to re-establish a dialogue through the Inzerillo family in the U.S," Francesco Messineo of the Italian Police said. "A dialogue that was never interrupted because the relationship between the American and the Italian Mafia is historic, based on long tradition. But there was certainly an attempt to re-establish that connection." Investigators believe mob clans wanted to collaborate on illegal commercial ventures such as money laundering and drug trafficking. Italian officials said the arrests were aimed at preventing these illegal activities, but they warned that other Mafia clans in Sicily oppose the return of the Inzerillo family to the island, and therefore were concerned about a new Mafia war. E-mail to a friend . CNN's Deborah Feyerick and Alessio Vinci contributed to this report.

outputs.L2:
NEW YORK (CNN) — Prosecutors said Thursday that a sweeping anti-Mafia operation spanning New York and Sicily had dismantled not just the leadership of the Gambino crime family, but much of the organization beneath it as well.

Among the 62 defendants named in the indictments is John “Jackie the Nose” D’Amico, pictured in 1992. Alleged members of the Gambino, Genovese and Bonanno families face a total of 80 counts, including murder, money laundering and unlawful gambling.

Benton Campbell, the U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of New York, said the allegations target the heart of the Gambino organization.

According to prosecutors, the family made money by extorting businesses in New York’s construction sector and labor unions. Gordon Heddell, inspector general of the U.S. Department of Labor, said several companies allegedly paid what amounted to a “mob tax” in exchange for protection and authorization to conduct business.

Queens County District Attorney Richard Brown said other counts concern a suspected illegal gambling operation. He alleged that Nicholas Corozzo, described as a Gambino captain, participated in a sports-betting business that used toll-free telephone lines, among other methods.

The indictment also accuses four Gambino members of eight murder-related offenses. One allegation involves the 1990 felony murder of Jose Delgado Rivera, who was fatally shot inside an armored truck during a robbery.

Campbell said the prosecution could now resolve long-unsolved crimes that authorities had not forgotten. The alleged criminal conduct extends back more than 30 years, he added.

A crucial part of Thursday’s Gambino operation was an undercover member of the New York attorney general’s Organized Crime Task Force who penetrated the family and secretly captured hundreds of hours of conversations, according to attorney general spokesman John Milgrim.

Police said 45 defendants were already being held. Arrests took place across New York City, Long Island and New Jersey.

New York Attorney General Andrew Cuomo compared organized crime to persistent weeds growing through society’s cracks and vowed that authorities would continue their efforts until it became a thing of the past.

The U.S. crackdown coincided with the detention of 77 suspected organized-crime figures in Italy. The Italian operation captured significant members of a powerful Sicilian clan connected to Mafia leader Salvatore Lo Piccolo, who was thought to have succeeded Bernardo Provenzano as the “boss of bosses.”

Investigators said Lo Piccolo, while seeking greater power, attempted to repair relationships with Mafia groups in New York after those connections were severed during the violent mob conflicts of the 1980s. The groups involved included New York’s Gambino family and Italy’s Inzerillo family.

Provenzano had been arrested in Corleone two years earlier.

Francesco Messineo of the Italian Police said it was clear that Palermo’s Mafia leadership wanted to renew communications with the United States through the Inzerillo family. He noted that links between the American and Italian Mafia had never completely disappeared because of their long, historic relationship, but said there was a definite effort to strengthen the connection again.

Authorities believed the criminal groups planned to cooperate in illicit businesses, including narcotics trafficking and money laundering. Italian officials said the arrests were intended to stop those ventures. They also cautioned that other Sicilian Mafia factions resisted the Inzerillos’ return to the island, raising fears that another mob war could erupt.

CNN’s Deborah Feyerick and Alessio Vinci contributed to the report.

The indictment also covered an illegal sports-gambling ring and eight murder-related offenses. Among the cases cited was the 1990 killing of armored-truck employee Jose Delgado Rivera.

outputs.L4:
Federal authorities announced a sweeping U.S.-Italian crackdown on organized crime, unsealing an 80-count indictment against 62 people accused of ties to the Gambino, Genovese, and Bonanno crime families. The coordinated operation, conducted with Italian law-enforcement officials, targeted alleged Mafia leaders, soldiers, associates, and business figures on both sides of the Atlantic.

The charges covered criminal activity stretching back roughly three decades. Prosecutors alleged that the defendants took part in extortion, illegal gambling, money laundering, racketeering, theft, and other schemes, as well as several murders. Authorities said the organizations used threats and violence to control businesses, collect debts, and protect illicit revenue.

A central part of the investigation involved an undercover agent who infiltrated organized-crime circles and recorded hundreds of hours of conversations. Those recordings, together with surveillance, informants, financial evidence, and other investigative work, gave authorities an unusually detailed view of the groups’ internal operations and alleged criminal plans.

Many of the defendants were arrested in coordinated raids in the United States, while Italian authorities carried out related actions overseas. Prosecutors said the operation disrupted longstanding connections between New York’s Mafia families and organized-crime figures in Sicily.

Officials described the case as a major blow to the Gambino family in particular. The arrests reached deeply into its leadership and affected several of its key crews and money-making operations. Although authorities cautioned that organized crime had not been eliminated, they said the prosecution significantly weakened the family’s ability to direct criminal activity.

Law-enforcement leaders also emphasized the historical reach of the case. By bringing charges connected to crimes committed over a period of about 30 years, they said, the investigation sought not only to dismantle current Mafia operations but also to hold alleged participants accountable for violence and corruption that had remained unresolved for decades.

# “Old Bridge” Raids Target Gambino Leaders in the United States and Italy

In February 2008, law-enforcement authorities in the United States and Italy carried out a coordinated series of Mafia raids aimed at the Gambino crime family in New York and its longstanding associates in Sicily. The investigation, known as **Operation Old Bridge**, resulted in dozens of arrests and charges involving murder, racketeering, extortion, drug trafficking and other organized-crime offenses.

Among the most prominent American targets were **John “Jackie the Nose” D’Amico**, then regarded by federal authorities as the Gambino family’s acting boss, and veteran Gambino leader **Nicholas Corozzo**.

D’Amico was arrested during the February 7 sweep. Investigators alleged that he had helped direct the Gambino organization while members of the family’s formal leadership were imprisoned or under close scrutiny. A longtime associate of former boss John Gotti, D’Amico had risen through the family’s ranks and was considered part of its senior administration.

Corozzo, an influential Gambino captain who had also been identified as a possible member of the family’s leadership, avoided capture during the initial raids. Authorities described him as a fugitive until he surrendered in May 2008. His brother, Joseph Corozzo, was another senior Gambino figure targeted in the broader prosecution.

Operation Old Bridge focused on renewed connections between New York’s Gambino family and the **Inzerillo clan of Palermo**. The Inzerillos had once been a powerful Sicilian Mafia faction but were driven from Sicily during the violent Mafia war of the early 1980s. Some members and associates relocated to the United States, where they maintained ties to the Gambinos. Investigators believed the weakening of their Sicilian rivals had created an opportunity for the Inzerillos to reestablish themselves in Palermo with help from American partners.

The American side of the operation was led by federal prosecutors and the FBI in New York, working with Italian police and anti-Mafia investigators. Arrests took place in the New York area and across Sicily. Authorities said the case demonstrated that the relationship between American and Sicilian organized crime remained active despite decades of prosecutions.

The indictments described a criminal network involved in construction-related extortion, illegal gambling, theft, drug trafficking and violence. Prosecutors also used cooperating witnesses, surveillance and recorded conversations to document meetings and business arrangements between figures on both sides of the Atlantic.

D’Amico later pleaded guilty to an extortion-related charge and received a prison sentence. Corozzo subsequently admitted participating in a racketeering conspiracy that included responsibility connected to a 1996 double murder and was sentenced to a substantially longer federal term.

The 2008 raids did not eliminate either the Gambino family or its overseas relationships, but they disrupted a significant attempt to strengthen the bridge between New York and Palermo. Operation Old Bridge also underscored a central feature of modern anti-Mafia enforcement: major organized-crime cases increasingly depended on sustained international cooperation rather than investigations confined to a single city or country.
